title: Reorder-based scheduler with prefetch & graceful timeouts for reranking endpoint
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Implement a reorder-first scheduler for the reranking endpoint that allows out-of-order execution of low-cost scoring lanes while ensuring strict deadline adherence for high-priority requests. The feature bundles three coordinated improvements: (1) request reordering to expose microbatching opportunities without inflating tail latency, (2) KV-prefetch hints for candidates in the scoring pipeline to reduce per-token stall when kernels are invoked, and (3) graceful soft timeouts that degrade scoring computation progressively (return partial scores, fall back to cached embeddings) instead of canceling requests outright. Primary goals are lower p95/p99 latency, improved throughput under mixed-priority workloads, and fewer user-facing timeouts during load spikes.
acceptance_criteria: p95 latency for 8k candidate rerank requests under baseline load reduced by at least 20% compared to current endpoint
p99 latency does not regress by more than 5% after enabling reordering under production-like skewed workloads
Endpoint returns a documented partial_score payload when soft timeout triggers, with schema backwards-compatible to current responses
No increase in memory usage per worker > 10% after enabling KV-prefetch across a 500-machine soak test
Automated integration tests and load scripts added and green in CI for runtime-1.23 branch
design_notes: Rationale: current strict FIFO scheduling leads to head-of-line blocking when expensive candidate scoring runs concurrently with cheap ones. Allowing conservative reordering permits grouping similar-cost requests into denser microbatches.

Scheduler model: maintain two priority lanes (hot and batchable). New arrival enters hot if request.deadline < token_estimate_threshold OR explicit customer priority. Otherwise candidate for reordering.
KV-prefetch: introduce an optional prefetch hint in request metadata. Prefetch warms L2 KV cache asynchronously using permissive memory budget and backpressure tokens.
Soft timeout strategy: progressively reduce scoring depth (e.g., top-k -> top-3 heuristics) and fallback to cached embedding similarity. Always return a 'score_confidence' field to signal quality.
Compatibility: keep existing API shape; partial responses use optional fields so older clients still parse. Document new fields in the API changelog.
Observability: add counters for reorders, prefetch hits/misses, and soft-timeout-triggered responses. Add a per-route microbatch histogram tagged by lane and batch size.
technical_approach: Step 1: Scheduler core - implement reorder buffer per worker with TTL-driven flush. Buffer size limited to token_estimate_budget and latency_headroom computed from request.deadline.
Step 2: Cost model - extend request profiler to predict kernel invocation cost (approx tokens * model_cost_coeff) using historical kernel timings and client-provided hints.
Step 3: Prefetch system - non-blocking prefetch tasks that populate KV cache. Use cooperative cancellation if request is dropped. Track prefetch budget per worker to avoid memory blow-up.

Step 4: Soft timeouts - add pipeline stages that can be truncated. Implement deterministic fallback ordering: reduce scorer depth -> use cached embeddings -> return partial score with explanation reason codes.
Step 5: Safety - enforce a strict max-reorder-window (50ms default) and an emergency bypass for SLA-critical customers where reordering is disabled via route config.
Step 6: Telemetry - emit granular events to tracing (span annotations) and add metrics for batch sizes, reorder latency, prefetch hit rate, and partial-return ratio.
Step 7: Testing - synthetic load tests with skewed cost distributions, chaos tests that drop prefetch, and long soak tests with mixture of priorities.
rollout_plan: Alpha: rollout to internal canary cluster with 10% of traffic. Observe metrics for 48 hours. Alert on p99 regressions >5% or prefetch memory > 10% of baseline.
Beta: enable for non-SLA public customers and test with real traffic for 7 days. Gradually increase traffic fraction to 40%.
GA: default on for all routes except those explicitly marked 'no-reorder' in route config. Provide toggle in Console to disable per-customer.
Rollback: immediate config flip to disable reorder and prefetch; soft timeouts are independent and can be toggled at runtime.
Migration: add migration job to backfill small-scale cached embeddings for high-volume customers to reduce fallback cost.
tests: Unit: reorder buffer eviction, TTL behavior, and prefetch budget accounting
Integration: end-to-end rerank flow with mocked kernel timings asserting batching and partial responses
Load: k6-based workload that simulates spikes and mixed candidate sizes; compare against baseline cluster
Soak: 72-hour soak under 2x baseline traffic to validate memory stability
Chaos: kill prefetch worker threads and assert graceful fallback to cached embeddings without client-visible errors
risks_and_mitigation: Risk: reordering could worsen tail latency if cost model misclassifies expensive requests. Mitigation: conservative defaults (small reorder window), continuous calibration job, and realtime feedback to the model profiler.
Risk: KV-prefetch increases memory footprint and GC pressure. Mitigation: per-worker quotas, LRU eviction, and runtime flags to disable prefetch when memory exceed threshold.
Risk: clients rely on strict determinism of rerank ordering. Mitigation: route-level opt-out and clear changelog entries; provide deterministic mode in configuration for affected customers.
Risk: operational complexity increases. Mitigation: add runbook steps, dashboard panels, and one-click rollback in Console.
open_questions: Q1: What is the safe default for reorder-window_ms across different instance types? Proposal: 25ms for V100-equivalent, 50ms for A100-equivalent (needs benchmarking).
Q2: Should prefetch be enabled by default for Dedicated customers who have isolated KV caches? Proposal: opt-in for first release, then evaluate.
Q3: How to quantify 'score_confidence' for downstream clients? Proposal: expose discrete buckets (high/medium/low) computed from beam depth and prefetch hit.
Q4: Do we need a server-side sacrifice strategy that sheds low-priority requests under extreme overload?
